name: SAMMA
lead: SAMMA is a mandelic acid condensation polymer, a compound built from repeating units of mandelic acid, the alpha hydroxy acid used in skincare peels.[1] SAMMA itself was developed as a candidate vaginal microbicide and contraceptive agent rather than a cosmetic, and it appears in skin-related discussion because of its link to mandelic acid chemistry.

Laboratory work reported that SAMMA blocks HIV and herpes simplex virus from binding to cells with little cytotoxicity, and it was licensed for development as a contraceptive microbicide.[2][3] People who look into mandelic acid for texture, pigmentation or acne-prone skin use the small-molecule acid in peels and serums; the polymer is a separate research compound with no published use on skin.[1]

Published SAMMA work consists of laboratory, animal and early preclinical studies from the 2000s, including an in vitro and rabbit-model assessment of its contraceptive, antimicrobial and safety properties.[5]

angle.text: SAMMA is not a skin product; people interested in mandelic acid for skin texture and pigmentation use the monomer in peels, while the polymer has been studied for infection prevention.

paras: SAMMA is a polymer formed by condensation of mandelic acid units. Mandelic acid (2-hydroxy-2-phenylacetic acid) is an aromatic alpha hydroxy acid first isolated in 1831 from bitter almond extract.[1] Unlike many antiviral polymers studied as microbicides, SAMMA is neither sulfonated nor sulfated, which the authors of the 2002 virology study noted as part of what made it structurally novel.[2]

In primary human macrophages and peripheral blood mononuclear cells, SAMMA was reported to be highly active against both CCR5- and CXCR4-using HIV isolates. It also inhibited infection of cervical epithelial cells by herpes simplex virus, with little or no cytotoxicity and a high selectivity index.[2] It was reported to block viral attachment by targeting the envelope glycoproteins gp120 (HIV) and gB-2 (HSV), and to inhibit HSV entry after attachment.[2]

A 2007 study found that SAMMA suppressed HIV transmission by dendritic cells, prevented HIV internalisation when the virus was pre-incubated with the compound, and blocked glycoprotein-mediated cell-cell fusion, which the authors took to indicate several mechanisms of action.[4]

Because it was developed as a combined contraceptive and antimicrobial, SAMMA was also examined for effects on sperm. It was reported to inhibit hyaluronidase and acrosin, induce acrosomal loss in sperm and act as a contraceptive in a rabbit model.[5] A follow-up study described a dose-dependent premature acrosome loss that required extracellular calcium, pointing to disrupted calcium signalling.[3]

A 2002 Journal of Virology paper described SAMMA as a candidate microbicide warranting further preclinical evaluation.[2] A companion Fertility and Sterility paper reported that it was not cytotoxic toward lactobacilli, host cells or spermatozoa, was not mutagenic, and had low acute oral toxicity in laboratory testing, and that it also acted on Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae to varying degrees.[5] The dendritic-cell study followed in 2007.[4] The sperm study describes SAMMA as licensed for development as a contraceptive microbicide.[3]

Mandelic acid is used in superficial chemical peels that are generally considered suitable across skin types. A 2022 review lists 40% mandelic acid among agents that improve pigmentation and texture, while the American Academy of Dermatology states that evidence is insufficient to recommend peels for acne.[1] People interested in the skin-related properties of the mandelic acid family are therefore looking at the monomer, not at SAMMA.
No studies found. Published SAMMA work is laboratory and preclinical, including cell culture, sperm assays and a rabbit contraceptive model.[2][3][4][5]

card.summary: A mandelic acid polymer studied as an antiviral microbicide, related to the mandelic acid used in skin-texture peels.
card.note: Laboratory-stage compound, not a skincare product.

quick.overview:
SAMMA is a polymer made from mandelic acid, the same acid used in gentle skincare peels.

It was developed as a vaginal microbicide and contraceptive candidate, so appearance uses refer to mandelic acid itself rather than SAMMA.
quick.mechanism: It blocks HIV and HSV from attaching to cells by targeting viral envelope proteins, and disrupts sperm acrosome function.
quick.risks: Only laboratory and preclinical studies exist; it is not a marketed product.
